claim: Rap1 is the main protein that binds double-stranded telomeric DNA in Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
source: Rap1 is the main protein that binds double-stranded telomeric DNA in Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field, supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: RAP1 is encoded by an essential gene.
source: Rap1 is the main protein that binds double-stranded telomeric DNA in Saccharomyces cerevisiae. Examination of the telomere functions of Rap1 is complicated by the fact that it also acts as a transcriptional regulator of hundreds of genes and is encoded by an essential gene.
evidence: The manuscript states that RAP1 is essential for viability, citing Shore and Nasmyth, 1987.

claim: tlc1-tm cells grow similar to wild-type cells.
source: tlc1-tm cells grow similar to wild-type cells, although depletion of Rap1 at telomeres causes defects in telomere length regulation and telomere capping.
evidence: This claim is supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Depletion of Rap1 at telomeres causes defects in telomere length regulation.
source: tlc1-tm cells grow similar to wild-type cells, although depletion of Rap1 at telomeres causes defects in telomere length regulation and telomere capping.
evidence: This is supported by Southern blot analysis showing longer and more heterogeneous telomeres in tlc1-tm cells (Figure 1B).

claim: Depletion of Rap1 at telomeres causes defects in telomere capping.
source: tlc1-tm cells grow similar to wild-type cells, although depletion of Rap1 at telomeres causes defects in telomere length regulation and telomere capping.
evidence: This is supported by telomere degradation observed in various mutant backgrounds and senescence assays.

claim: Rif2 can still associate with Rap1-depleted tlc1-tm telomeres.
source: Rif2 is a protein normally recruited to telomeres by Rap1, but we show that Rif2 can still associate with Rap1-depleted tlc1-tm telomeres, and that this association is required to inhibit telomere degradation by the MRX complex.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-qPCR data showing Rif2 association with tlc1-tm telomeres (Figure 4A).

claim: Rif2 association with Rap1-depleted tlc1-tm telomeres is required to inhibit telomere degradation by the MRX complex.
source: Rif2 is a protein normally recruited to telomeres by Rap1, but we show that Rif2 can still associate with Rap1-depleted tlc1-tm telomeres, and that this association is required to inhibit telomere degradation by the MRX complex.
evidence: This is supported by Southern blot analysis showing extensive telomere degradation in rif2∆ tlc1-tm cells (Figure 5B) and rescue by deletion of RAD50 (Figure 6B).

claim: Rif2 and the Ku complex work in parallel to prevent tlc1-tm telomere degradation.
source: Rif2 and the Ku complex work in parallel to prevent tlc1-tm telomere degradation; tlc1-tm cells lacking Rif2 and the Ku complex are inviable.
evidence: This is supported by the inviability of rif2∆ yku70∆ tlc1-tm triple mutants (Figure 6E).

claim: tlc1-tm cells lacking Rif2 and the Ku complex are inviable.
source: Rif2 and the Ku complex work in parallel to prevent tlc1-tm telomere degradation; tlc1-tm cells lacking Rif2 and the Ku complex are inviable.
evidence: This is demonstrated by tetrad dissection showing no viable rif2∆ yku70∆ tlc1-tm spores (Figure 6E).

claim: The tlc1-tm template region is 3′-CACCUAAACCACACAC-5′.
source: The tlc1-tm template region is 3′-CACCUAAACCACACAC-5′, resulting in [(TG)0–4TGG]nATTTGG mutant telomeric repeats (Chang et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated directly in the text with a citation to Chang et al., 2007.

claim: The tlc1-tm template results in [(TG)0–4TGG]nATTTGG mutant telomeric repeats.
source: The tlc1-tm template region is 3′-CACCUAAACCACACAC-5′, resulting in [(TG)0–4TGG]nATTTGG mutant telomeric repeats (Chang et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated directly in the text with a citation to Chang et al., 2007.

claim: The lack of the GGG motif in the mutant repeat sequence should disrupt Rap1 binding.
source: The lack of the GGG motif in the mutant repeat sequence should disrupt Rap1 binding, yet the tlc1-tm mutant grows similar to a wild-type strain (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is based on knowledge of Rap1's consensus binding sequence which contains an invariable CCC core.

claim: Telomeres in the tlc1-tm mutant are on average longer and more heterogeneous in length than in wild-type strains.
source: Telomeres in the tlc1-tm mutant are on average longer and more heterogeneous in length than in wild-type strains (Figure 1B)
evidence: This is directly shown by Southern blot analysis in Figure 1B.

claim: The telomere profile of tlc1-tm is much less dramatically altered compared to most other TLC1 mutants with altered template sequences.
source: but the telomere profile of tlc1-tm is much less dramatically altered compared to most other TLC1 mutants with altered template sequences (Förstemann et al., 2003; Lin et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a comparative statement based on citations to previous studies.

claim: Rap1 has a consensus DNA-binding sequence of 5′-CACCCAYACMYM-3′ containing an invariable CCC core.
source: Rap1 has a consensus DNA-binding sequence of 5′-CACCCAYACMYM-3′ (where Y is C or T, and M is A or C) containing an invariable CCC core (Graham and Chambers, 1994; Lieb et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Graham and Chambers, 1994 and Lieb et al., 2001.

claim: Binding of Rap1 is substantially reduced at the VII-L-MUT telomere.
source: Binding of Rap1 is substantially reduced at the VII-L-MUT telomere (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Rap1 is more modestly reduced at Y′ telomeres due to the retention of some wild-type repeats at native telomeres.
source: Rap1 is more modestly reduced at Y′ telomeres due to the retention of some wild-type repeats at native telomeres.
evidence: This is inferred from the ChIP-qPCR data and the understanding that native telomeres retain some wild-type sequence.

claim: Rap1 shows a very poor binding capacity to the tlc1-tm oligonucleotides compared to the wild-type telomeric sequence.
source: We find that Rap1 shows a very poor binding capacity to the tlc1-tm oligonucleotides compared to the wild-type telomeric sequence (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by EMSA data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Cdc13 is the main sequence-specific single-stranded telomeric DNA binding protein in S. cerevisiae.
source: Cdc13 is the main sequence-specific single-stranded telomeric DNA binding protein in S. cerevisiae (Nugent et al., 1996).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Nugent et al., 1996.

claim: Cdc13 requires a minimum of 11 nucleotides of GT-rich sequence for full binding affinity, with only three bases—forming a GNGT motif—recognized with high specificity.
source: Cdc13 requires a minimum of 11 nucleotides of GT-rich sequence for full binding affinity, with only three bases—forming a GNGT motif—recognized with high specificity (Eldridge et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Eldridge et al., 2006.

claim: The GNGT motif is present in the tlc1-tm mutant sequence.
source: The GNGT motif is present in the tlc1-tm mutant sequence, so Cdc13 binding should not be altered.
evidence: This is inferred from the sequence of tlc1-tm repeats.

claim: Cdc13 associates equally well with both wild-type and mutant telomeres.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, we find that Cdc13 associates equally well with both wild-type and mutant telomeres (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The essential function of Rap1 is likely linked to its ability to bind nontelomeric sites in the genome where it acts as a transcriptional regulator of several hundred genes.
source: However, the essential function of Rap1 is likely linked to its ability to bind nontelomeric sites in the genome where it acts as a transcriptional regulator of several hundred genes (Azad and Tomar, 2016).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Azad and Tomar, 2016.

claim: S. cerevisiae strains expressing a mutant telomerase that adds vertebrate TTAGGG telomeric repeats are devoid of Rap1.
source: In addition, S. cerevisiae strains expressing a mutant telomerase that adds vertebrate TTAGGG telomeric repeats are devoid of Rap1, indicating that Rap1 is not essential for telomere capping (Alexander and Zakian, 2003; Brevet et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Alexander and Zakian, 2003 and Brevet et al., 2003.

claim: Rap1 is not essential for telomere capping.
source: In addition, S. cerevisiae strains expressing a mutant telomerase that adds vertebrate TTAGGG telomeric repeats are devoid of Rap1, indicating that Rap1 is not essential for telomere capping (Alexander and Zakian, 2003; Brevet et al., 2003).
evidence: This is inferred from the viability of strains with TTAGGG repeats that lack Rap1.

claim: Tbf1 binds to the vertebrate repeats and is able to regulate telomere length homeostasis in a Rap1-independent manner.
source: In these strains, Tbf1 binds to the vertebrate repeats and is able to regulate telomere length homeostasis in a Rap1-independent manner (Alexander and Zakian, 2003; Berthiau et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Alexander and Zakian, 2003 and Berthiau et al., 2006.

claim: There is no change in the levels of Tbf1 at tlc1-tm telomeres compared to wild-type telomeres.
source: We find no change in the levels of Tbf1 at tlc1-tm telomeres compared to wild-type telomeres by ChIP-qPCR (Figure 1G)
evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Neither wild-type nor mutant telomere sequences contain the RCCCT Tbf1 consensus binding sequence.
source: consistent with neither wild-type nor mutant telomere sequences containing the RCCCT Tbf1 consensus binding sequence (Preti et al., 2010)
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Preti et al., 2010.

claim: The loss of Rap1 is not compensated by recruitment of Tbf1.
source: indicating that the loss of Rap1 is not compensated by recruitment of Tbf1.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of change in Tbf1 levels at tlc1-tm telomeres.

claim: The Tbf1 association observed at the native Y′ telomeres is due to the presence of TTAGGG repeats at subtelomeric regions.
source: The Tbf1 association observed at the native Y′ telomeres is due to the presence of TTAGGG repeats at subtelomeric regions (Brigati et al., 1993)
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Brigati et al., 1993.

claim: The Tbf1 association observed at the artificial VII-L telomere is likely due to the presence of several RCCCT motifs in the adjacent sequence.
source: while the association observed at the artificial VII-L telomere is likely due to the presence of several RCCCT motifs in the adjacent sequence (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of RCCCT motifs shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The decreased binding of Rap1 to tlc1-tm sequences likely explains the long, heterogeneous-sized telomeres in tlc1-tm strains.
source: The decreased binding of Rap1 to tlc1-tm sequences likely explains the long, heterogeneous-sized telomeres in tlc1-tm strains because Rap1 negatively regulates telomerase through what is called the 'protein counting' model.
evidence: This is an inference based on the protein counting model and the observed telomere phenotype.

claim: Rap1 negatively regulates telomerase through the 'protein counting' model.
source: because Rap1 negatively regulates telomerase through what is called the 'protein counting' model. This model posits that Rap1, through its recruitment of Rif1 and Rif2, inhibits telomerase; the longer a telomere is, the more Rap1, Rif1, and Rif2 will be present, and the stronger the inhibition of telomerase will be (Marcand et al., 1997; Levy and Blackburn, 2004).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Marcand et al., 1997 and Levy and Blackburn, 2004.

claim: The protein counting model posits that Rap1, through its recruitment of Rif1 and Rif2, inhibits telomerase.
source: This model posits that Rap1, through its recruitment of Rif1 and Rif2, inhibits telomerase; the longer a telomere is, the more Rap1, Rif1, and Rif2 will be present, and the stronger the inhibition of telomerase will be (Marcand et al., 1997; Levy and Blackburn, 2004).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Marcand et al., 1997 and Levy and Blackburn, 2004.

claim: The longer a telomere is, the more Rap1, Rif1, and Rif2 will be present, and the stronger the inhibition of telomerase will be.
source: This model posits that Rap1, through its recruitment of Rif1 and Rif2, inhibits telomerase; the longer a telomere is, the more Rap1, Rif1, and Rif2 will be present, and the stronger the inhibition of telomerase will be (Marcand et al., 1997; Levy and Blackburn, 2004).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Marcand et al., 1997 and Levy and Blackburn, 2004.

claim: Reduced binding of Rap1 would cause tlc1-tm telomeric sequences to not be recognized as telomeric in terms of Rap1-mediated telomere length regulation.
source: Reduced binding of Rap1 would cause tlc1-tm telomeric sequences to not be recognized as telomeric in terms of Rap1-mediated telomere length regulation.
evidence: This is a hypothesis tested by the experiment shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The size of the telomere VII-L terminal restriction fragment increased in size when seeded with tlc1-tm sequence, with the magnitude of the increase roughly equivalent to the size of the tlc1-tm telomeric seed sequence.
source: In both cases, the size of the telomere VII-L terminal restriction fragment increased in size, with the magnitude of the increase roughly equivalent to the size of the tlc1-tm telomeric seed sequence, indicating that this sequence is not being sensed by the Rap1 protein counting mechanism (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Southern blot analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: tlc1-tm telomeric sequence is not being sensed by the Rap1 protein counting mechanism.
source: indicating that this sequence is not being sensed by the Rap1 protein counting mechanism (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is inferred from the Southern blot data in Figure 2A.

claim: At wild-type telomeres, telomerase extends only a subset of telomeres in each cell cycle, with a strong preference for the extension of short telomeres.
source: At wild-type telomeres, telomerase extends only a subset of telomeres in each cell cycle, with a strong preference for the extension of short telomeres (Teixeira et al., 2004; Strecker et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Teixeira et al., 2004 and Strecker et al., 2017.

claim: At tlc1-tm telomeres, telomere extension frequency is dramatically increased, with nearly all (92%) of the telomeres being extended during a single-cell cycle.
source: At tlc1-tm telomeres, we find that telomere extension frequency is dramatically increased, with nearly all (92%) of the telomeres being extended during a single-cell cycle (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by iSTEX data shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: The depletion of Rap1 at tlc1-tm telomeres causes them to all be recognized as short telomeres in need of elongation.
source: This observation is consistent with the protein counting model; the depletion of Rap1 at tlc1-tm telomeres causes them to all be recognized as short telomeres in need of elongation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the iSTEX data and the protein counting model.

claim: The increase in telomere extension frequency of tlc1-tm telomeres is much more dramatic than the increase seen in rif1∆, rif2∆, and pif1-m2 cells.
source: The increase in telomere extension frequency of tlc1-tm telomeres is much more dramatic than the increase seen in rif1∆, rif2∆, and pif1-m2 cells (Teixeira et al., 2004; Stinus et al., 2017)
evidence: This is a comparative statement based on citations to previous studies.

claim: Ablation of Rap1 leads to readily detectable telomere degradation within a few hours.
source: Ablation of Rap1 leads to readily detectable telomere degradation within a few hours (Vodenicharov et al., 2010)
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Vodenicharov et al., 2010.

claim: While decreased Rap1 at tlc1-tm telomeres may favor their extension by telomerase, increased degradation may limit the length of tlc1-tm telomeres.
source: so we hypothesized that while decreased Rap1 at tlc1-tm telomeres may favor their extension by telomerase, increased degradation may limit the length of tlc1-tm telomeres.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observed telomere phenotype and known effects of Rap1 depletion.

claim: Cells containing mutant telomeres senesced rapidly, only ~40 population doublings after telomerase loss.
source: We found that cells containing mutant telomeres senesced rapidly, only ~40 population doublings after telomerase loss (Figure 3A, est2Δ tlc1-tm* and tlc1Δ*).
evidence: This is demonstrated by senescence assay data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Upon loss of telomerase, mutant telomeres became extremely heterogeneous and degraded.
source: We examined the telomere length of cells that had undergone ~30 population doublings after isolation of the haploid spores and found that, upon loss of telomerase, mutant telomeres became extremely heterogeneous and degraded (i.e., a continuous smear of telomeric DNA-hybridizing signal extending from the wells to the bottom; Figure 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Southern blot analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Rap1, through its C-terminal domain, recruits Rif1, Rif2, Sir3, and Sir4 to telomeres.
source: Rap1, through its C-terminal domain, recruits Rif1, Rif2, Sir3, and Sir4 to telomeres (Hardy et al., 1992; Wotton and Shore, 1997; Moretti et al., 1994).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Hardy et al., 1992, Wotton and Shore, 1997, and Moretti et al., 1994.

claim: Rif1 and Sir4 recruitment to the VII-L-MUT telomere is reduced compared to the VII-L-WT telomere.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, we find that Rif1 and Sir4 recruitment to the VII-L-MUT telomere is reduced compared to the VII-L-WT telomere (to 16% for Rif1 and 31% for Sir4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The recruitment of neither Rif2 nor Sir3 is affected at tlc1-tm telomeres.
source: Surprisingly, the recruitment of neither Rif2 nor Sir3 is affected.
evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Rif2 can interact with the Xrs2 and Rad50 subunits of the MRX complex.
source: Rif2 can interact with the Xrs2 and Rad50 subunits of the MRX complex (Hirano et al., 2009; Hailemariam et al., 2019; Roisné-Hamelin et al., 2021)
evidence: This is stated with citations to Hirano et al., 2009, Hailemariam et al., 2019, and Roisné-Hamelin et al., 2021.

claim: Rif2 can interact directly with double-strand DNA.
source: Rif2 can also interact directly with double-strand DNA (Cassani et al., 2016; Hailemariam et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Cassani et al., 2016 and Hailemariam et al., 2019.

claim: Sir3 possesses multiple domains that can interact with histones.
source: Sir3 possesses multiple domains that can interact with histones (Gartenberg and Smith, 2016).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Gartenberg and Smith, 2016.

claim: Rif2 and Sir3 may associate to tlc1-tm telomeres via Rap1-independent mechanisms.
source: Thus, Rif2 and Sir3 may associate to tlc1-tm telomeres via Rap1-independent mechanisms.
evidence: This is inferred from the maintained association of Rif2 and Sir3 at tlc1-tm telomeres despite reduced Rap1.

claim: Rap1, through its recruitment of the Rif and Sir proteins, represses the transcription of non-coding telomeric repeat-containing RNA (TERRA).
source: Rap1, through its recruitment of the Rif and Sir proteins, represses the transcription of non-coding telomeric repeat-containing RNA (TERRA) (Iglesias et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Iglesias et al., 2011.

claim: There is no change in TERRA abundance in tlc1-tm cells.
source: However, we find no change in TERRA abundance in tlc1-tm cells (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Rap1, through its recruitment of the Sir complex, mediates the transcriptional silencing of subtelomeric genes.
source: Rap1, through its recruitment of the Sir complex, also mediates the transcriptional silencing of subtelomeric genes (Moretti et al., 1994).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Moretti et al., 1994.

claim: There is no difference in URA3 silencing between VII-L-WT and VII-L-MUT.
source: In both assays, we find no difference between VII-L-WT and VII-L-MUT, indicating that the reduced levels of Rap1 and Sir4 at tlc1-tm telomeres still allow functional silencing.
evidence: This is demonstrated by 5-FOA growth assays (Figure 4C) and RT-qPCR (Figure 4D).

claim: The reduced levels of Rap1 and Sir4 at tlc1-tm telomeres still allow functional silencing.
source: In both assays, we find no difference between VII-L-WT and VII-L-MUT, indicating that the reduced levels of Rap1 and Sir4 at tlc1-tm telomeres still allow functional silencing.
evidence: This is inferred from the URA3 silencing data.

claim: Rap1 regulates telomere length homeostasis through its recruitment of Rif1, Rif2, and Sir4.
source: Rap1 regulates telomere length homeostasis through its recruitment of Rif1, Rif2, and Sir4.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Rif1 and Rif2 negatively regulate telomerase.
source: Rif1 and Rif2 negatively regulate telomerase (Hardy et al., 1992; Wotton and Shore, 1997; Levy and Blackburn, 2004).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Hardy et al., 1992, Wotton and Shore, 1997, and Levy and Blackburn, 2004.

claim: Sir4 functions in a pathway to recruit telomerase to telomeres.
source: In contrast, Sir4 functions in a pathway to recruit telomerase to telomeres (Hass and Zappulla, 2015).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Hass and Zappulla, 2015.

claim: Deletion of SIR4 results in a small decrease in telomere length in TLC1 cells.
source: Deletion of SIR4 results in a small decrease in telomere length in TLC1 cells, as expected (Hass and Zappulla, 2015), but no noticeable change in tlc1-tm cells (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Southern blot analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Deletion of SIR4 causes no noticeable change in telomere length in tlc1-tm cells.
source: Deletion of SIR4 results in a small decrease in telomere length in TLC1 cells, as expected (Hass and Zappulla, 2015), but no noticeable change in tlc1-tm cells (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Southern blot analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Deletion of RIF1 increases telomere length in both TLC1 and tlc1-tm cells.
source: Deletion of RIF1 increases telomere length in both TLC1 and tlc1-tm cells (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is demonstrated by Southern blot analysis shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Deletion of RIF2 causes dramatic degradation of tlc1-tm telomeres.
source: Deletion of RIF2 causes dramatic degradation of tlc1-tm telomeres, with a continuous smear of telomeric DNA-hybridizing signal observed (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is demonstrated by Southern blot analysis shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Rif2 has an important role in protecting tlc1-tm telomeres.
source: This finding, along with the observation that Rif2 is still present at tlc1-tm telomeres (Figure 4A), indicates that Rif2 has an important role in protecting tlc1-tm telomeres.
evidence: This is inferred from the telomere degradation phenotype in rif2∆ tlc1-tm cells.

claim: The extensive smear of telomeric DNA was still observed in dnl4∆ rif2∆ tlc1-tm and rad52∆ rif2∆ tlc1-tm triple mutants, but was reduced in intensity, especially at low molecular weight, in rad52∆ rif2∆ tlc1-tm.
source: The extensive smear was still observed in dnl4∆ rif2∆ tlc1-tm and rad52∆ rif2∆ tlc1-tm triple mutants, but was reduced in intensity, especially at low molecular weight, in rad52∆ rif2∆ tlc1-tm (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Southern blot analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: rif2∆ tlc1-tm cells grow poorly.
source: rif2∆ tlc1-tm cells grow poorly, and this growth defect is exacerbated by additional deletion of RAD52
evidence: This is demonstrated by colony size measurements and growth assays shown in Figure 5D and E.

claim: The growth defect of rif2∆ tlc1-tm cells is exacerbated by additional deletion of RAD52.
source: rif2∆ tlc1-tm cells grow poorly, and this growth defect is exacerbated by additional deletion of RAD52; rad52∆ rif2∆ tlc1-tm spores mostly fail to germinate, and those that do grow even more poorly than rif2∆ tlc1-tm (Figure 5D and E)
evidence: This is demonstrated by colony size measurements and growth assays shown in Figure 5D and E.

claim: rad52∆ rif2∆ tlc1-tm spores mostly fail to germinate, and those that do grow even more poorly than rif2∆ tlc1-tm.
source: rad52∆ rif2∆ tlc1-tm spores mostly fail to germinate, and those that do grow even more poorly than rif2∆ tlc1-tm (Figure 5D and E)
evidence: This is demonstrated by colony size measurements and growth assays shown in Figure 5D and E.

claim: Rad52-mediated HR helps cope with rif2∆ tlc1-tm uncapped telomeres.
source: suggesting that Rad52-mediated HR helps cope with rif2∆ tlc1-tm uncapped telomeres.
evidence: This is inferred from the severe growth defect of rad52∆ rif2∆ tlc1-tm cells.

claim: rad52∆ tlc1-tm cells have longer telomeres than tlc1-tm cells.
source: rad52∆ tlc1-tm cells also have longer telomeres than tlc1-tm cells (Figure 5C), indicating that HR is important for maintaining tlc1-tm telomeres.
evidence: This is demonstrated by Southern blot analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: HR is important for maintaining tlc1-tm telomeres.
source: indicating that HR is important for maintaining tlc1-tm telomeres.
evidence: This is inferred from the longer telomeres in rad52∆ tlc1-tm cells.

claim: rif1∆ rif2∆ and rif1∆ rif2∆ tlc1-tm cells have very similar telomere profiles: very long telomeres but without the extensive degradation seen in rif2∆ tlc1-tm cells.
source: Interestingly, rif1∆ rif2∆ and rif1∆ rif2∆ tlc1-tm cells have very similar telomere profiles: very long telomeres but without the extensive degradation seen in rif2∆ tlc1-tm cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Southern blot analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: TEL1 is epistatic to RIF2 with respect to telomere length regulation.
source: TEL1 is epistatic to RIF2 with respect to telomere length regulation; while rif2∆ cells have long telomeres, tel1∆ and rif2∆ tel1∆ cells have very short telomeres (Craven and Petes, 1999).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Craven and Petes, 1999.

claim: Deletion of TEL1 shortens the telomeres of tlc1-tm cells.
source: Deletion of TEL1 shortens the telomeres of tlc1-tm cells, but does not affect the telomere profile of rif2∆ tlc1-tm cells (Figure 5B)
evidence: This is demonstrated by Southern blot analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Deletion of TEL1 does not affect the telomere profile of rif2∆ tlc1-tm cells.
source: Deletion of TEL1 shortens the telomeres of tlc1-tm cells, but does not affect the telomere profile of rif2∆ tlc1-tm cells (Figure 5B)
evidence: This is demonstrated by Southern blot analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Rif2 does not inhibit Tel1 to prevent the degradation of tlc1-tm telomeres.
source: indicating that Rif2 does not inhibit Tel1 to prevent the degradation of tlc1-tm telomeres.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of effect of TEL1 deletion on rif2∆ tlc1-tm telomere profile.

claim: Rif2 attenuates Tel1 activity at telomeres by inhibiting the MRX complex.
source: Recent studies have shown that Rif2 attenuates Tel1 activity at telomeres by inhibiting the MRX complex (consisting of Mre11, Rad50, and Xrs2), which is responsible for recruiting Tel1 to telomeres (Hailemariam et al., 2019; Sabourin et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Hailemariam et al., 2019 and Sabourin et al., 2007.

claim: The MRX complex is responsible for recruiting Tel1 to telomeres.
source: Recent studies have shown that Rif2 attenuates Tel1 activity at telomeres by inhibiting the MRX complex (consisting of Mre11, Rad50, and Xrs2), which is responsible for recruiting Tel1 to telomeres (Hailemariam et al., 2019; Sabourin et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Hailemariam et al., 2019 and Sabourin et al., 2007.

claim: Rif2 discharges the ATP-bound state of Rad50, thereby making the MRX complex incapable of activating Tel1.
source: Rif2 discharges the ATP-bound state of Rad50, thereby making the MRX complex incapable of activating Tel1 (Hailemariam et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Hailemariam et al., 2019.

claim: Rif2 enhancement of Rad50 ATPase activity limits MRX-mediated tethering of DNA ends during double-strand break (DSB) repair.
source: Similarly, Rif2 enhancement of Rad50 ATPase activity limits MRX-mediated tethering of DNA ends during double-strand break (DSB) repair (Cassani et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Cassani et al., 2016.

claim: Rif2 inhibits MRX-mediated resection of telomeric DNA ends.
source: Rif2 also inhibits MRX-mediated resection of telomeric DNA ends (Bonetti et al., 2010a; Bonetti et al., 2010b).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Bonetti et al., 2010a and Bonetti et al., 2010b.

claim: Rif2 inhibition of the MRX complex involves a direct interaction between the BAT/MIN motif of Rif2 with the ATPase domain of Rad50.
source: Rif2 inhibition of the MRX complex involves a direct interaction between the BAT/MIN motif of Rif2 with the ATPase domain of Rad50 (Roisné-Hamelin et al., 2021; Khayat et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Roisné-Hamelin et al., 2021 and Khayat et al., 2021.

claim: Mre11 is about fivefold more associated with the VII-L-MUT telomere in comparison with the VII-L-WT telomere.
source: Consistent with this idea, we find that Mre11 is about fivefold more associated with the VII-L-MUT telomere in comparison with the VII-L-WT telomere (Figure 6A)
evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 6A.
